claim: A dual reporter H9 human embryonic stem cell line was generated that enables sorting of neural progenitors and neurons.
source: To investigate progenitor and neuron-specific gene regulatory programs, we generated a dual reporter H9 human embryonic stem cell (hESC) line that enables sorting of neural progenitors and neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: The text explicitly states the generation of the dual reporter line and its purpose. Figure 1A provides visual representation of the experimental design.

claim: The stop codon of one allele of SOX2 was replaced with P2A-EGFP to label neural progenitors.
source: To label neural progenitors, we replaced the stop codon of one allele of the pan-neural progenitor marker gene SOX2 with P2A-EGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text describes the genetic modification strategy, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows the genotyping results confirming the modification.

claim: dTomato driven by human Synapsin1 promoter was inserted in the AAVS1 safe harbor locus to label neurons.
source: On the other hand, to label neurons, we inserted dTomato driven by human Synapsin1 (hSYN1) promoter in the AAVS1 safe harbor locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text describes the insertion strategy, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows genotyping PCR results confirming the insertion.

claim: Brain organoids were generated using a previously published organoid culture protocol enriched in dorsal telencephalic tissue.
source: Using this dual reporter line, we generated brain organoids enriched in dorsal telencephalic tissue using a previously published organoid culture protocol (Esk et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) to recapitulate the key stages of corticogenesis, when multipotent progenitors give rise to diverse excitatory neurons of distinct layer identities.
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Esk et al., 2020) and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing the protocol schematic.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed broad expression of EGFP in the progenitor zone and dTomato in the neuronal zone.
source: Immunostaining for EGFP and dTomato confirmed broad expression of the fluorophores in the progenitor and neuronal zones, respectively (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results, and Figures 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D show the fluorescence patterns in organoid sections.

claim: EGFP expression matched SOX2 expression in the ventricular zone.
source: First, it confirmed expression of EGFP and dTomato in the progenitor-rich ventricular zone (VZ) (SOX2), and the surrounding neuron-rich region (NeuN), respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The text describes co-localization analysis, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C shows immunostaining results.

claim: Both EGFP and dTomato fluorescent proteins marked the entire cell body including long cellular processes.
source: It was observed that in accordance with their cytoplasmic localization, both fluorescent proteins marked the entire cell body and therefore also the long cellular processes characteristic of radial glia and neurons.
evidence: The text describes the observed localization pattern of the fluorescent proteins based on imaging data.

claim: Some cells expressed both EGFP and dTomato, indicative of a transition state between progenitors and neurons.
source: A few cells expressed both EGFP and dTomato probably indicative of a transition state (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The text describes the observation and provides an interpretation. Figure 1—figure supplement 2D shows cells with double positive staining.

claim: Some EGFP positive cells were located outside the typical VZ and stained positive for EOMES, a marker for intermediate progenitors.
source: Furthermore, some EGFP positive cells were also located outside the typical VZ and stained positive for EOMES, a marker for intermediate progenitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D shows EGFP and EOMES co-staining.

claim: Organoids were dissociated and cells were sorted by fluorescence activated cell sorting at days 40, 60, 90, and 120.
source: Dissociation of the organoids followed by fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) confirmed the occurrence of EGFP positive (EGFP+) and dTomato positive (dTomato+) cell populations across different stages of organoid development (days 40, 60, 90, and 120) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text describes the FACS procedure and timepoints. Figure 1—figure supplement 3A shows FACS gating and sorted populations.

claim: An EGFP/dTomato double positive cell population was detected by FACS.
source: Additionally, an EGFP/dTomato double positive cell population was detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text describes FACS results, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A shows the double positive population.

claim: The double positive population at days 40 and 60 matched a transition stage between progenitors and neurons based on RNA-seq analysis.
source: RNA-seq-based whole transcriptome analysis of these sorted cell populations and subsequent principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that the double positive population at days 40 and 60 matched a transition stage between progenitors and neurons, while at days 90 and 120 it was more similar to EGFP+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The text describes PCA results from RNA-seq data. Figure 1—figure supplement 3B shows the PCA plot with the double positive population clustering.

claim: SOX2::EGFP+ cells and hSYN1::dTomato+ cells clustered separately in PCA and showed transcriptomic signatures of progenitors and neurons, respectively.
source: PCA showed that SOX2::EGFP+ cells and hSYN1::dTomato+ cells clustered separately and showed transcriptomic signatures of progenitors and neurons, respectively (PC1, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: The text describes PCA results. Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B show the PCA plots and loading scores.

claim: Samples separated according to organoid developmental stages with little batch effect in the transcriptome analysis.
source: These samples further separated according to the organoid developmental stages with little batch effect (PC2, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: The text describes PCA results. Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B show PC2 separating by developmental stage.

claim: 6740 proteins were detected by mass spectrometry of the sorted cell populations.
source: In total, 6740 proteins were detected by mass spectrometry of the sorted cell populations.
evidence: The text explicitly states the number of proteins detected in the proteomics analysis.

claim: The proteome of sorted neurons and progenitor cells segregated according to cell class.
source: Initial analysis confirmed that similar to the transcriptome, the proteome of sorted neurons (hSYN1::dTomato+) and progenitor cells (SOX2::EGFP+) segregated according to the cell class (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: The text describes PCA results from proteomics data. Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and D show the PCA plots.

claim: Segregation by age was less striking in the proteome potentially due to technical limitations of TMT-labeling experiments.
source: Segregation by age was less striking potential due to technical limitations reported for TMT-labeling experiments, such as ratio compression (Savitski et al., 2013) and channel cross-talk (Searle and Yergey, 2020).
evidence: The text provides an interpretation of the proteomics results and cites technical limitations from previous publications (Savitski et al., 2013; Searle and Yergey, 2020).

claim: EGFP and dTomato expression matched the expression of endogenous SOX2 and SYN1.
source: Transcriptome and proteome analysis (Figure 1C–E) confirmed that EGFP and dTomato expression matched the expression of endogenous SOX2 and SYN1, thus highlighting the suitability of our dual reporter strategy (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The text describes the comparison of reporter and endogenous gene expression. Figures 1C and D show the expression patterns.

claim: The SOX2::EGFP+ population encompassed all different classes of cortical progenitors including ventricular radial glia, intermediate progenitors, and outer radial glia.
source: Furthermore, this analysis revealed that the SOX2::EGFP+ population encompassed all different classes of cortical progenitors including ventricular radial glia (expression of SOX1, PAX6), intermediate progenitors (EOMES), as well as outer radial glia (HOPX).
evidence: The text describes the analysis of marker gene expression in the SOX2::EGFP+ population.

claim: Markers of ventricular radial glia were expressed at all stages in the SOX2::EGFP+ population.
source: While the markers of ventricular radial glia were expressed at all stages, markers of intermediate progenitors and outer radial glia showed enrichment at days 60 and 90, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text describes temporal expression patterns. Figure 1C shows the expression of progenitor markers over time.

claim: The hSYN1::dTomato+ population included excitatory neurons of all different cortical layers.
source: Similarly, the hSYN1::dTomato+ population included excitatory neurons of all different cortical layers and followed the expected temporal expression patterns (Figure 1D), with deep-layer markers (TBR1, BCL11B) being expressed before upper-layer markers (SATB2, CUX2).
evidence: The text describes the analysis of neuronal marker expression. Figure 1D shows the expression of neuronal markers over time.

claim: Deep-layer neuronal markers were expressed before upper-layer markers in the hSYN1::dTomato+ population.
source: Similarly, the hSYN1::dTomato+ population included excitatory neurons of all different cortical layers and followed the expected temporal expression patterns (Figure 1D), with deep-layer markers (TBR1, BCL11B) being expressed before upper-layer markers (SATB2, CUX2).
evidence: The text describes temporal expression patterns. Figure 1D shows the sequential expression of layer markers.

claim: Dorsal telencephalic fate was confirmed by high expression of FOXG1 and EMX2.
source: The enrichment of dorsal telencephalic fate was confirmed by the expression of above stated markers of cortical progenitors and neurons along with high expression of FOXG1 and EMX2 (Figure 1E) and undetectable levels of ventral markers (NKX2.1, LHX6) (TPM values below 1).
evidence: The text describes marker expression analysis. Figure 1E shows the expression of dorsal telencephalic markers.

claim: Ventral markers NKX2.1 and LHX6 showed undetectable levels (TPM values below 1).
source: The enrichment of dorsal telencephalic fate was confirmed by the expression of above stated markers of cortical progenitors and neurons along with high expression of FOXG1 and EMX2 (Figure 1E) and undetectable levels of ventral markers (NKX2.1, LHX6) (TPM values below 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states the TPM values for ventral markers.

claim: The double positive population at days 40 and 60 showed expression of progenitor and neuronal markers at intermediate levels.
source: In line with the PCA, the excluded double positive population at days 40 and 60 showed expression of progenitor and neuronal markers at levels intermediate to those in SOX2::EGFP+ population and hSYN1::dTomato+ population. This is indicative of a transition state between progenitors and neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: The text describes marker expression analysis. Figure 1—figure supplement 5A shows the expression patterns in the double positive population.

claim: At days 90 and 120, the double positive population showed mixed marker expression including high expression of general progenitor and outer radial glia markers, enrichment of gliogenic markers, and moderate expression of neuronal markers.
source: However, at days 90 and 120, the double positive population showed mixed marker expression including high expression of general progenitor and outer radial glia markers, enrichment of gliogenic markers, as well as moderate expression of neuronal markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: The text describes marker expression analysis. Figure 1—figure supplement 5A shows the expression patterns.

claim: Extracellular matrix proteins (laminins, collagens) and cell adhesion proteins were lost upon tissue dissociation and FACS.
source: We observed that mainly extracellular matrix (laminins, collagens) and cell adhesion proteins (e.g. AGRN, VCAN), as well as markers for astrocytes (GFAP) and choroid plexus (TTR) were lost upon tissue dissociation and dual reporter-based FACS (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: The text describes the comparison of intact organoids to sorted cells. Figure 1—figure supplement 6B shows enrichment analysis of proteins lost during dissociation.

claim: Markers for astrocytes (GFAP) and choroid plexus (TTR) were lost upon tissue dissociation and FACS.
source: We observed that mainly extracellular matrix (laminins, collagens) and cell adhesion proteins (e.g. AGRN, VCAN), as well as markers for astrocytes (GFAP) and choroid plexus (TTR) were lost upon tissue dissociation and dual reporter-based FACS (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: The text describes the comparison results. Figure 1—figure supplement 6B shows enrichment analysis.

claim: A limited correlation was observed between absolute mRNA and protein levels, comparable between cell classes and developmental time points.
source: Similar to a previous report (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011), we observed only a limited correlation between absolute mRNA and protein levels, which seemed comparable between cell classes and developmental time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: The text describes correlation analysis and cites a previous report (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011). Figure 1—figure supplement 7A shows correlation plots.

claim: Almost 80% of the variation in the combined transcriptome and proteome datasets was explained by the omics method before normalization.
source: Given the very different measurement units of RNA-seq and Mass-spec, a PCA on the combined datasets revealed that almost 80% of the variation was explained by the omics method (PC1, Figure 1—figure supplement 7B) and not by cell class or developmental time point highlighting the importance of data normalization.
evidence: The text describes PCA results before normalization. Figure 1—figure supplement 7B shows the PCA plot.

claim: After z-score normalization, the combined datasets grouped by cell classes and developmental age and not by the omics method.
source: PCA of the combined datasets confirmed that the scaled data grouped by cell classes and developmental age and not by the omics method (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: The text describes PCA results after normalization. Figures 1F and G show the PCA plot and loading scores.

claim: Out of 6714 genes, regression models were successfully fit for 5978 genes.
source: Out of the 6714 genes, we could successfully fit regression models for 5978 genes, 3668 of which showed significant temporal expression changes between cell classes on RNA and/or protein levels.
evidence: The text explicitly states the number of genes for which regression models were fit.

claim: 3668 genes showed significant temporal expression changes between cell classes on RNA and/or protein levels.
source: Out of the 6714 genes, we could successfully fit regression models for 5978 genes, 3668 of which showed significant temporal expression changes between cell classes on RNA and/or protein levels.
evidence: The text explicitly states the number of genes with significant temporal changes.

claim: 3368 genes were classified into nine modules by hierarchical clustering.
source: In the end, a total of 3368 genes were classified into nine modules (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The text states the number of genes clustered into modules. Figures 2A and B show the clustering results.

claim: 2310 genes were considered as 'not clustered' and 736 genes as 'not fit'.
source: The remaining 2310 genes were considered as 'not clustered' and 736 genes for which the first regression fit failed as 'not fit' (Figure 1—figure supplement 7D and E and Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: The text states the number of genes not clustered or not fit. Figure 1—figure supplement 7D and E show the expression patterns of these genes.

claim: Genes that were not clustered or not fit were enriched in house-keeping genes, including core components of the proteasome, spliceosome, and RNA polymerase.
source: These genes lacked specific expression patterns and were enriched in house-keeping genes, including core components of the proteasome, spliceosome, and RNA polymerase (Figure 1—figure supplement 7F).
evidence: The text describes enrichment analysis results. Figure 1—figure supplement 7F shows GO term enrichment.

claim: Modules 1 and 2 showed higher relative expression in progenitors than neurons across all time points.
source: Modules 1 and 2 showed higher relative expression in the progenitors than neurons across all time points and were enriched in DNA replication and cell activation-related genes, respectively (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The text describes module expression patterns. Figure 2B shows the expression trends, and Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B show GO enrichment.

claim: Module 1 is enriched in DNA replication-related genes.
source: Modules 1 and 2 showed higher relative expression in the progenitors than neurons across all time points and were enriched in DNA replication and cell activation-related genes, respectively (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The text describes GO enrichment results. Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B show the enriched GO terms.

claim: Module 2 is enriched in cell activation-related genes.
source: Modules 1 and 2 showed higher relative expression in the progenitors than neurons across all time points and were enriched in DNA replication and cell activation-related genes, respectively (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The text describes GO enrichment results. Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B show the enriched GO terms.

claim: For module 2, progenitor-enriched expression increased with time, in line with the observation that many outer radial glia markers were members of this cluster.
source: For module 2, progenitor-enriched expression increased with time, in line with the observation that many outer radial glia markers were members of this cluster.
evidence: The text describes the temporal expression pattern of module 2 and provides an interpretation based on marker gene membership.

claim: Modules 7, 8, and 9 showed higher expression in neurons than progenitors across all time points.
source: Genes in modules 7, 8, and 9 showed higher expression in neurons than progenitors across all time points.
evidence: The text describes module expression patterns based on the analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Module 7 is enriched in genes related to mitochondrial respiration.
source: Module 7 was enriched in genes related to mitochondrial respiration (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), which is in agreement with the metabolic shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation observed during neurogenesis (Iwata and Vanderhaeghen, 2021).
evidence: The text describes GO enrichment results and cites a previous publication (Iwata and Vanderhaeghen, 2021). Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B show the enriched GO terms.

claim: The metabolic shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation is observed during neurogenesis.
source: Module 7 was enriched in genes related to mitochondrial respiration (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), which is in agreement with the metabolic shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation observed during neurogenesis (Iwata and Vanderhaeghen, 2021).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Iwata and Vanderhaeghen, 2021) describing this metabolic shift.

claim: Modules 8 and 9 are enriched in axonal and pre- and postsynaptic genes.
source: Modules 8 and 9 were enriched in axonal and pre- and postsynaptic genes (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The text describes GO enrichment results. Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B show the enriched GO terms.

claim: In 'C' modules (1, 2, 7, 8, 9), global relative expression of RNA and protein followed largely similar trends.
source: Importantly, in 'C' modules, global relative expression of RNA and protein followed largely similar trends, indicating that the regulation of these genes might occur via cell class-specific transcription or transcript retention and decay.
evidence: The text describes the observation from Figure 2B and provides an interpretation of the regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Module 4 expression decreased with time and the average RNA trends were similar for progenitors and neurons, but progenitors expressed relatively higher amounts of protein.
source: In module 4, expression decreased with time and the average RNA trends for these genes were similar for progenitors and neurons. However, progenitors expressed relatively higher amounts of protein.
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern observed in Figure 2B.

claim: Module 4 includes known early fate specification genes such as FEZF2 and genes related to glycolysis.
source: This module includes known early fate specification genes such as FEZF2, as well as genes related to glycolysis, a process more prominent in progenitors (Iwata and Vanderhaeghen, 2021).
evidence: The text describes the gene composition of module 4 and cites a previous publication (Iwata and Vanderhaeghen, 2021).

claim: Module 6 genes were expressed more at later stages with similar RNA trends for progenitors and neurons, but protein levels were higher in neurons.
source: In contrast, module 6 genes were expressed more at later stages. The average RNA trends of these genes were similar for progenitors and neurons, but protein levels were higher in neurons (Figure 2B), suggesting less efficient translation or reduced protein stability in progenitors over neurons.
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern observed in Figure 2B and provides an interpretation.

claim: Module 6 includes upper-layer fate regulators such as SATB2 and CUX2.
source: This cluster includes upper-layer fate regulators such as SATB2 and CUX2.

source: Genes from module 3 showed considerably higher transcript levels in progenitors than neurons, although protein levels between the two cell classes were more similar.

claim: Module 5 genes showed opposite patterns for RNA and protein relation in progenitors and neurons.
source: Lastly, module 5 genes showed opposite patterns for RNA and protein relation in progenitors and neurons. The relative RNA levels showed a temporal increase in the two cell classes, with late-stage neurons expressing even higher amounts than corresponding progenitors. Despite this trend, the relative protein levels were higher in progenitors than neurons and with the difference being highest at early stages.
evidence: The text describes the expression pattern observed in Figure 2B.

claim: Module 5 is enriched in RNA-binding proteins like DEAD box proteins and proteins important for rRNA processing and ribosome biogenesis.
source: This module is enriched in RBPs like DEAD box proteins and proteins important for rRNA processing and ribosome biogenesis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).

claim: Modules with high cell class-specific expression ('C' modules) showed higher correlation between relative RNA and protein abundance than modules with broader expression patterns ('T' and 'A' modules).
source: Modules that show a high cell class-specific expression ('C' modules) showed a higher correlation than modules with broader expression patterns ('T' and 'A' modules) reflected in the coherency between RNA and protein trends.

claim: Modules 1 and 9 showcased high numbers of RBP motifs that were significantly enriched or depleted in the 3'UTR.
source: Modules 1 and 9, whose member genes showed most cell class-specific expression, showcased high numbers of RBP motifs that were significantly enriched or depleted in the 3'UTR (Figure 3B).
evidence: The text describes RBP motif enrichment analysis results. Figure 3B shows the number of enriched/depleted motifs per module.

claim: There was a reciprocal relationship between motifs enriched in the progenitor modules 1 and 2 and the neuronal module 9.
source: Upon comparing over- and underrepresented motifs among different modules, we observed that there was a reciprocal relationship between motifs enriched in the progenitor modules 1 and 2 and the neuronal module 9 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The text describes the comparison of RBP motif enrichment across modules. Figure 3C shows the enrichment patterns.

claim: Motifs for the RBP RBFOX1 were enriched in the 3'UTRs of module 9.
source: For instance, we observed that motifs for the RBP RBFOX1, which was shown to promote neuronal expression of synaptic genes (Lee et al., 2016), were enriched in the 3'UTRs of module 9 (Figure 3C) in line with the enrichment for gene ontology (GO) terms for synaptic genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: The text describes RBP motif enrichment and cites a previous publication (Lee et al., 2016). Figure 3C shows the enrichment.

claim: RBFOX1 was shown to promote neuronal expression of synaptic genes.
source: For instance, we observed that motifs for the RBP RBFOX1, which was shown to promote neuronal expression of synaptic genes (Lee et al., 2016), were enriched in the 3'UTRs of module 9 (Figure 3C) in line with the enrichment for gene ontology (GO) terms for synaptic genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Lee et al., 2016) describing the function of RBFOX1.

claim: ELAVL1 protein was shown to be important to maintain progenitor state by stabilization of key cell cycle and notch signaling transcripts.
source: As another example, ELAVL1 protein was shown to be important to maintain progenitor state by stabilization of key cell cycle and notch signaling transcripts (García-Domínguez et al., 2011).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (García-Domínguez et al., 2011) describing the function of ELAVL1.

claim: Motifs for the ELAVL family, especially ELAVL1, were enriched in the 3'UTRs of modules 1 and 2.
source: In line with this, motifs for the ELAVL family, especially ELAVL1, were enriched in the 3'UTRs of modules 1 and 2 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1) that showed enrichment for GO terms for cell cycle and neural progenitor genes (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Modules 6 and 8 showed significantly higher density of miRNA-binding sites in the 3'UTR.
source: Module-wise analysis showed a significantly higher density of miRNA-binding sites for genes of modules 6 and 8, indicating that the expression of some fate regulators and neuronal genes is regulated by miRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

source: Compared to all other modules, module 3 transcripts were overall shorter in all these features, whereas modules 8 and 9 seemed to have longer 5' and 3'UTRs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).

claim: Modules 8 and 9 have longer 5' and 3'UTRs.

evidence: The text describes transcript length analysis. Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F show the length distributions.

evidence: The text describes MFE analysis. Figure 3—figure supplement 1H shows the MFE distributions.

claim: Neurons are enriched for longer genes that are susceptible to differential transcriptional regulation.
source: Previous studies have shown that neurons are particularly enriched for longer genes that are susceptible to differential transcriptional regulation (Gabel et al., 2015; King et al., 2013; McCoy et al., 2018; Miura et al., 2013; Sugino et al., 2014).
evidence: The text cites multiple previous publications (Gabel et al., 2015; King et al., 2013; McCoy et al., 2018; Miura et al., 2013; Sugino et al., 2014) describing this observation.

evidence: The text describes AU-rich element analysis and cites a previous publication (Ma et al., 1997). Figure 3—figure supplement 1J shows the AU element fraction.

source: On the other hand, module 9 has significantly less AU-rich elements in the 3'UTR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J) that corroborates the observed depletion of binding motifs for the ELAV-like family (Figure 3C), which is a major binding partner of AU-rich sequences (Ma et al., 1997).

source: This was especially striking for module 3 which was enriched in ribosomal proteins and eukaryotic translation initiation factors that contain the unique regulatory 5'TOP motif in their 5'UTR (Figure 3F and G; Figure 3—source data 3; Cockman et al., 2020; Philippe et al., 2020; Yamashita et al., 2008).

source: At protein level, however, a relative difference in the immunostaining in progenitor- and neuron-rich regions was not detectable (Figure 4B).

claim: RPL5 and RPL11 show higher transcript levels in progenitors than neurons, but protein levels were not different between the two cell classes in sparsely labeled organoids.
source: Indeed, we could validate that RPL5 and RPL11 show higher transcript levels in progenitors than neurons, but protein levels were not different between the two cell classes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The text describes quantification results from sparsely labeled organoids. Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E show the quantifications.

claim: 5'TOP transcripts show higher expression in neuroepithelial, radial glia and intermediate progenitor cells compared to neurons at gestational weeks 6–10 in human fetal brain scRNA-seq data.
source: To confirm that this observation is not brain organoid-specific and is also found in vivo, we analyzed a published human fetal brain scRNA-seq dataset (Eze et al., 2021). Similar to our results, 5'TOP transcripts show higher expression in neuroepithelial, radial glia and intermediate progenitor cells compared to neurons at gestational weeks 6–10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The text describes analysis of published data (Eze et al., 2021). Figure 4—figure supplement 1F shows the expression scores.

claim: In progenitors (SOX2+), the 5'TOP reporter showed more cells with lower tagBFP fluorescence compared to the non-5'TOP reporter.
source: In progenitors (SOX2+), the 5'TOP reporter showed more cells with lower tagBFP fluorescence compared to the non-5'TOP reporter (Figure 4D).
evidence: The text describes flow cytometry results. Figure 4D shows the cumulative distribution plots.

claim: In neurons (TUJ1+), the 5'TOP reporter showed the tendency toward higher tagBFP expressing cells compared to the non-5'TOP reporter.
source: On the other hand, in neurons (TUJ1+), the 5'TOP reporter showed the tendency toward higher tagBFP expressing cells compared to the non-5'TOP reporter (Figure 4E).
evidence: The text describes flow cytometry results. Figure 4E shows the cumulative distribution plots.

claim: The presence of 5'TOP motif lowers the effective tagBFP protein yield in progenitors.
source: This was observed consistently between different human pluripotent stem cell lines (H9 and Rozh-5 backgrounds) and experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D and E), indicating that in general, the presence of 5'TOP motif lowers the effective tagBFP protein yield in progenitors.
evidence: The text describes the consistent observation across multiple experiments. Figure 4—figure supplement 3D and E show additional experimental replicates.

claim: 5'TOP RNAs localize to stress granules during cellular stress.
source: 5'TOP translation is mainly known to be regulated during cellular stress (Cockman et al., 2020). During stress conditions, 5'TOP RNAs localize to stress granules (SGs), which are dense RNA-protein condensates (Damgaard and Lykke-Andersen, 2011; Wilbertz et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites previous publications (Cockman et al., 2020; Damgaard and Lykke-Andersen, 2011; Wilbertz et al., 2019) describing 5'TOP RNA localization during stress.

claim: More G3BP1-positive puncta with higher fluorescence intensity were observed in sodium arsenite-treated organoids compared to control organoids.
source: As expected, more G3BP1-positive puncta (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A) with higher fluorescence intensity (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B) were observed in the NaAs-treated organoids.
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results. Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and B show the images and quantifications.

claim: G3BP1-positive puncta were observed in the VZ of control organoids.
source: However, the occurrence of weak G3BP1 puncta in control organoids, particularly in the VZ was supportive of our hypothesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results. Figure 4—figure supplement 4C shows the quantification of granule density.

claim: Control organoids did not show generally high levels of phospho-EIF2, indicating the control organoid tissue is not under acute stress.
source: Analyzing the distribution of another stress marker phospho-EIF2 confirmed that unlike NaAs-treated organoids, the control organoids did not show generally high levels of phospho-EIF2. This observation showed that the control organoid tissue is not under acute stress (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E and F).
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results. Figure 4—figure supplement 4E and F show the images and quantifications.

claim: RPL5 and RPL11 transcripts localize to mScarlet-positive stress granule-like structures in the VZ.
source: Furthermore, we performed RNA-FISH and observed localization of RPL5 and RPL11 transcripts to these mScarlet-positive SGL structures in the VZ (Figure 4F).
evidence: The text describes RNA-FISH results. Figure 4F shows the FISH images with G3BP1-mScarlet granules.

claim: The intensity of the FISH signal for RPL5 and RPL11 was similar in the stress granule-like structures and the cytoplasm.
source: The intensity of the FISH signal was similar in the SGL structures and the cytoplasm (Figure 4G), which would suggest that only a small fraction of the mRNA is sequestered in the granules, in agreement with reduced protein yield and not a translational block.
evidence: The text describes quantification of FISH signal intensity. Figure 4G shows the quantification.

claim: RPL5 and RPL11 transcripts were strongly enriched in G3BP1-positive granules in sodium arsenite-treated organoids.
source: In contrast, RPL5 and RPL11 transcripts were strongly enriched in G3BP1-positive granules in NaAs-treated organoids (Figure 4—figure supplement 5D) in line with previous studies (Damgaard and Lykke-Andersen, 2011; Wilbertz et al., 2019).
evidence: The text describes FISH results and cites previous studies (Damgaard and Lykke-Andersen, 2011; Wilbertz et al., 2019). Figure 4—figure supplement 5D shows the quantification.

claim: 5'TOP RNAs are more stable in progenitors than neurons.
source: This analysis revealed that 5'TOP RNAs are more stable in the progenitors than neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 6A) and that this difference is most prominent at day 40 (Figure 4—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: The text describes relative stability analysis. Figure 4—figure supplement 6A and B show the stability estimates.

claim: The mTOR pathway is a major regulator of 5'TOP translation, which is inhibited upon mTOR pathway inhibition.
source: The mTOR pathway is a major regulator of 5'TOP translation, which is inhibited upon mTOR pathway inhibition (Cockman et al., 2020).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Cockman et al., 2020) describing mTOR regulation of 5'TOP translation.

claim: Phospho-4E-BP1 staining showed uniform distribution across the organoid tissue, indicating generally active mTOR signaling.
source: The uniform distribution of phospho-4E-BP1 (p4E-BP1) across the tissue indicated generally active mTOR signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results. Figure 5—figure supplement 1A shows the immunostaining image.

claim: Phospho-S6 staining showed enrichment outside the VZ in neuronal regions.
source: However, as reported previously for organoid and fetal samples (Andrews et al., 2020; Eze et al., 2021) phospho-S6 (pS6) staining showed enrichment outside the VZ in neuronal regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results and cites previous publications (Andrews et al., 2020; Eze et al., 2021). Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows the immunostaining image.

claim: TSC2-/- organoids showed significantly higher signal of pS6 throughout the VZ compared to control tissue, indicating overactivation of the TSC2-mTOR pathway.
source: Furthermore, TSC2-/- organoids showed significantly higher signal of pS6 throughout the VZ when compared to the control tissue (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), indicating overactivation of the TSC2-mTOR pathway.
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results. Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G show the images and quantifications.

claim: 5'TOP transcripts showed overall increased levels in the high-polysome fractions in TSC2-/- organoids compared to control organoids.
source: When specifically analyzing 5'TOP transcripts we found overall increased levels in the high-polysome fractions in TSC2-/- organoids compared to control organoids, whereas similar levels were detected in the low-polysome and monosome fractions (Figure 5E).
evidence: The text describes polysome profiling results. Figure 5E shows the MA plots.

claim: The relative fraction of 5'TOP transcripts actively translated in high-polysomes over the translationally less active monosomes was increased in TSC2-/- over control organoids.
source: Accordingly, the relative fraction of 5'TOP transcripts actively translated in high-polysomes over the translationally less active monosomes was increased in TSC2-/- over control organoids (Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The text describes polysome profiling analysis. Figure 5F shows the log2 fold change.

claim: RPL5 and RPL11 protein levels were increased in the VZ of TSC2-/- organoids.
source: To confirm that the upregulation of 5'TOP transcripts in the polysome fraction results in increased protein levels, we performed RNA-FISH and immunostainings in TSC2-/- and control organoids for RPL5 and RPL11. While we could not detect differences in their RNA levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B), we observed an increase in protein levels in the VZ of TSC2-/- organoids in H9 as well as Rozh-5 background (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: The text describes FISH and immunostaining results. Figures 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and D show the quantifications.

claim: Genes with higher translation in TSC2-/- organoids were significantly enriched in modules 4, 7, and 9.
source: For genes, which were significantly higher in the high-polysome fraction of TSC2-/- over those of control, we observed a significant enrichment for modules 4, 7, and 9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The text describes overrepresentation analysis. Figure 5—figure supplement 4A shows the enrichment results.

claim: Genes with lower translation in TSC2-/- organoids were significantly enriched in progenitor-specific modules 1 and 2.
source: In contrast, the genes which were less translated in the TSC2-/- organoids over control were significantly enriched in progenitor-specific modules 1 and 2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The text describes overrepresentation analysis. Figure 5—figure supplement 4A shows the enrichment results.

claim: TSC2-/- organoids showed a significant reduction in the fraction of EGFP+ cells (progenitors) and a significant increase in the fraction of dTomato+ cells (neurons).
source: In agreement with the polysome profiling data from Rozh-5 organoids, we observed a significant reduction in the fraction of EGFP+ cells (progenitors) and a significant increase in the fraction of dTomato+ cells (neurons) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The text describes flow cytometry results. Figure 5—figure supplement 4D shows the quantifications.

claim: The ratio of dTomato+ cells to EGFP+ was increased in TSC2-/-, indicative of increased differentiation.
source: Overall, the ratio of dTomato+ cells to EGFP+ was increased in the TSC2-/-, indicative of an increased differentiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The text describes flow cytometry results and provides an interpretation. Figure 5—figure supplement 4D shows the quantifications.

claim: Precocious occurrence of the glial marker S100B was observed in TSC2-/- tissue at day 40.
source: Apart from an increase in neuronal markers, we also observed precocious occurrence of the glial marker S100B in the TSC2-/- tissue at day 40 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4E), reinforcing our observation that the progenitors are shifted toward a precocious differentiation state.
evidence: The text describes immunostaining results. Figure 5—figure supplement 4E shows the immunostaining images.

claim: 5'TOP transcripts skip the global translational inhibition during mitosis.
source: During mitosis, 5'TOP transcripts skip the global translational inhibition (Park et al., 2016), whereas in stress context these transcripts are the first ones to be translationally inhibited to conserve the resources and energy of the cell by downregulating translation (Cockman et al., 2020; Fonseca et al., 2014; Meyuhas and Kahan, 2015).
evidence: The text cites previous publications (Park et al., 2016; Cockman et al., 2020; Fonseca et al., 2014; Meyuhas and Kahan, 2015) describing 5'TOP regulation during mitosis and stress.

claim: In stress context, 5'TOP transcripts are the first ones to be translationally inhibited to conserve the resources and energy of the cell.
source: During mitosis, 5'TOP transcripts skip the global translational inhibition (Park et al., 2016), whereas in stress context these transcripts are the first ones to be translationally inhibited to conserve the resources and energy of the cell by downregulating translation (Cockman et al., 2020; Fonseca et al., 2014; Meyuhas and Kahan, 2015).
evidence: The text cites previous publications (Cockman et al., 2020; Fonseca et al., 2014; Meyuhas and Kahan, 2015) describing 5'TOP regulation during stress.

claim: The energetic state of a cell can impact the formation of stress granule-like structures under physiological conditions.
source: A recent report suggests that the energetic stage of a cell can impact the formation of SGLs under physiological conditions (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The text cites a recent publication (Wang et al., 2022) describing the impact of energetic state on SGL formation.

claim: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is physiologically active at early stages of mouse corticogenesis to promote neurogenesis.
source: Another stress-related pathway, the unfolded protein response (UPR) is physiologically active at early stages of mouse corticogenesis to promote neurogenesis (Laguesse et al., 2015).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Laguesse et al., 2015) describing UPR activity during mouse corticogenesis.

claim: Overactivation of the UPR beyond its physiological levels affects the generation of intermediate progenitors in the mouse and human cortical tissue, resulting in a microcephalic phenotype.
source: Overactivation of the UPR beyond its physiological levels affects the generation of intermediate progenitors in the mouse and human cortical tissue, resulting in a microcephalic phenotype (Esk et al., 2020; Laguesse et al., 2015; Pașca et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites previous publications (Esk et al., 2020; Laguesse et al., 2015; Pașca et al., 2019) describing the effects of UPR overactivation.

claim: Translational regulation of 5'TOP transcripts plays a role in germline stem cell differentiation in Drosophila.
source: Recently, a role of the translational regulation of 5'TOP transcripts has been suggested in germline stem cell differentiation in Drosophila (Martin et al., 2022) and in mouse adult neurogenesis (Baser et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites a recent publication (Martin et al., 2022) describing 5'TOP regulation in Drosophila germline stem cells.

claim: Translational regulation of 5'TOP transcripts plays a role in mouse adult neurogenesis.
source: Recently, a role of the translational regulation of 5'TOP transcripts has been suggested in germline stem cell differentiation in Drosophila (Martin et al., 2022) and in mouse adult neurogenesis (Baser et al., 2019).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Baser et al., 2019) describing 5'TOP regulation in mouse adult neurogenesis.

claim: Ribosome availability is a critical factor determining the translation of mRNAs with complex 5'UTRs with secondary structures.
source: Ribosome availability is proposed to be a critical factor determining the translation of mRNAs with complex 5'UTRs with secondary structures (Hetman and Slomnicki, 2019).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Hetman and Slomnicki, 2019) proposing this relationship.

claim: Reduced ribosome biogenesis and availability is indicated at an early stage of mouse corticogenesis.
source: Reduced ribosome biogenesis and availability is also indicated at an early stage of mouse corticogenesis (Chau et al., 2018; Harnett et al., 2021).
evidence: The text cites previous publications (Chau et al., 2018; Harnett et al., 2021) describing reduced ribosome biogenesis in mouse corticogenesis.

claim: A global regulation of the translational machinery has been reported for mid-gestation stages of mouse corticogenesis, with gradual reduction in the translational efficiency of 5'TOP genes and the availability of ribosomes.
source: A global regulation of the translational machinery has been recently reported for mid-gestation stages of mouse corticogenesis, with gradual reduction in the translational efficiency of 5'TOP genes and the availability of ribosomes (Harnett et al., 2021).
evidence: The text cites a recent publication (Harnett et al., 2021) describing global regulation of the translational machinery in mouse corticogenesis.

claim: The role of the mTOR pathway in progenitor proliferation and neuronal morphology and function is well documented.
source: The role of the mTOR pathway in progenitor proliferation and neuronal morphology and function is well documented (Switon et al., 2017).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Switon et al., 2017) documenting the role of mTOR.

claim: Early radial glia show lower mTOR activity in interphase in human brain organoid tissue.
source: Our results in human brain organoid tissue show that early radial glia show lower mTOR activity in interphase.
evidence: The text describes the observation from the immunostaining results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Studies using mouse, 2D neuronal cultures and cortical spheroid cultures have reported a drop in mTOR activity during early stages of corticogenesis.
source: Studies using mouse, 2D neuronal cultures and cortical spheroid cultures have also reported a drop in mTOR activity during early stages of corticogenesis (Blair et al., 2018; Blair et al., 2017; Chau et al., 2018).
evidence: The text cites previous publications (Blair et al., 2018; Blair et al., 2017; Chau et al., 2018) reporting reduced mTOR activity.

claim: Analysis of human fetal transcriptome of early stages has suggested a similar trend of reduced mTOR activity.
source: Analysis of human fetal transcriptome of early stages has also suggested a similar trend (Eze et al., 2021).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Eze et al., 2021) analyzing human fetal transcriptome.

claim: Human outer radial glia exhibit higher mTOR activity, both in primary fetal tissue and in brain organoids.
source: On the other hand, human outer radial glia that arise at later stages of corticogenesis exhibit higher mTOR activity, both in primary fetal tissue and in brain organoids (Andrews et al., 2020).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Andrews et al., 2020) describing higher mTOR activity in outer radial glia.

claim: Mutations in mTOR pathway-related genes are associated with tuberous sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia, and megalencephaly.
source: Mutations in mTOR pathway-related genes are associated with many genetic disorders such as tuberous sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia, and megalencephaly (Crino, 2016).
evidence: The text cites a previous publication (Crino, 2016) describing the association of mTOR pathway mutations with genetic disorders.

claim: The integrated dataset describes cell class- and developmental stage-specific gene expression at both RNA and protein level.
source: Finally, our integrated dataset describes cell class- and developmental stage-specific gene expression, both at RNA and protein level and is available to browse for the wider community in the form of a R-based Shiny app (https://organoid.multiomics.vbc.ac.at).
evidence: The text explicitly states the availability of the dataset as a Shiny app.

claim: This is the first time RNA and protein datasets for human corticogenesis have been integrated.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time RNA and protein datasets for human corticogenesis have been integrated.
evidence: The text explicitly states this is the first integration of RNA and protein datasets for human corticogenesis.

claim: The gene regulation of SATB2 observed during mouse corticogenesis also holds true in humans.
source: For instance, our data indicates that the gene regulation of the upper-layer marker SATB2 observed during mouse corticogenesis (Harnett et al., 2021) also holds true in humans.
evidence: The text describes the observation from the dataset and cites a previous publication (Harnett et al., 2021) describing SATB2 regulation in mouse.
